{{Short description|On eigenvalues of random matrices}}
In [[probability theory]], more specifically the study of [[random matrices]], the '''circular law''' concerns the distribution of [[eigenvalues]] of an <math>n \times n</math> [[random matrix]] with [[independent and identically distributed random variables|independent and identically distributed entries]] in the limit 
<math>n \to \infty</math>.

It asserts that for any sequence of [[random matrices|random {{math|''n'' &times; ''n''}} matrices]] whose entries are [[independent and identically distributed random variables]], all with [[expected value|mean]] zero and [[variance]] equal to {{math|1/''n''}}, the limiting spectral distribution is the [[uniform distribution (continuous)|uniform distribution]] over the unit disc.

== Ginibre ensembles ==
Let <math>G_N</math> be a Ginibre ensemble matrix of size <math>N \times N</math>.

The real Ginibre ensemble is defined by sampling each entry [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|IID]] form the standard normal distribution. That is, we have <math>G_{ij} \sim \mathcal N \left(0, 1\right) </math>.

The complex Ginibre ensemble is defined as <math>G_{ij} \sim \mathcal N \left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right) + i\mathcal N \left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right) </math>.

The quaternionic Ginibre ensemble is defined as <math>G_{ij} \sim \mathcal N \left(0, \frac{1}{4}\right) + i\mathcal N \left(0, \frac{1}{4}\right) + j\mathcal N \left(0, \frac{1}{4}\right) + k\mathcal N \left(0, \frac{1}{4}\right) </math>. Although, since the quaternion number system is inconvenient, it is usually not sampled as a quaternion matrix of shape <math>n \times n</math>, but rather as a complex matrix of shape <math>2N \times 2N</math>, divided into <math>2 \times 2</math> blocks of form <math>\begin{bmatrix}
z & w \\
-\bar{w} & \bar{z}
\end{bmatrix}</math>, such that each <math>z, w</math> is IID sampled from <math>\mathcal N \left(0, \frac{1}{4}\right) + i\mathcal N \left(0, \frac{1}{4}\right) </math>.

The probability measure of the Ginibre ensemble satisfies<math display="block">\ln \rho(G) = -\frac\beta 2 \sum_{i j} |G_{ij}|^2 - \ln Z_{\beta, N} = \frac\beta 2 \operatorname{Tr}(GG^*) - \ln Z_{\beta, N}</math>where

* <math>\beta = 1, 2, 4</math> respectively for the real, complex, and quaternionic cases;
* <math>Z_{\beta, N}</math> is a [[Partition function (statistical mechanics)|normalization factor]];
* <math>\operatorname{Tr}</math> is the [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]];
* <math>^*</math> is the [[matrix adjoint]].
The most commonly used case is <math>\beta = 2</math>, and when "Ginibre ensemble" is spoken of, it by default means the <math>\beta = 2</math> case.

By analogy with the gaussian ensembles, the cases of <math>\beta = 1, 2, 4</math> are also called the GinOE, GinUE, GinSE, meaning "Ginibre Orthogonal/Unitary/Symplectic Ensemble".

== Spectral distribution ==

=== Probability density function ===
For <math>\beta = 2</math>, the eigenvalues of <math>G_N  </math> are distributed according to<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Meckes |first=Elizabeth |title=The Eigenvalues of Random Matrices |date=2021-01-08 |class=math.PR |eprint=2101.02928}}</ref><math display="block">\rho_N\left(z_1, \ldots, z_N\right)=\frac{1}{Z} \exp \left(-\sum_{k=1}^N\left|z_k\right|^2\right) \prod_{1 \leq j<k \leq N}\left|z_j-z_k\right|^2</math>where <math>Z = \pi^N \prod_{k=1}^N k!</math> is a [[Selberg integral]]. Ignoring the term <math>Z</math>, the rest of the formula can be obtained by exploiting the biunitary symmetry of the ensemble. That is, for any unitary <math>U, V</math>, the ensemble <math>UGV</math> has the same distribution.

For <math>\beta = 4</math>, the <math>2N \times 2N</math> matrix has complex eigenvalues that come in conjugate pairs. Index the eigenvalues as <math>z_1, \dots, z_n, z_{n+1}, \dots, z_{2n}</math> such that <math>z_{j} = \bar z_{n+j}</math>, then<ref name=":1">{{cite arXiv | last1=Byun | first1=Sung-Soo | last2=Forrester | first2=Peter J. | title=Progress on the study of the Ginibre ensembles I: GinUE | date=2022 | class=math-ph | eprint=2211.16223 }}</ref><math display="block">\rho_N\left(z_1, \ldots, z_N\right) \propto 
\prod_{l=1}^N e^{-2\left|z_l\right|^2}\left|z_l-\bar{z}_l\right|^2 
\prod_{1 \leq j<k \leq N}\left|z_k-z_j\right|^2\left|z_k-\bar{z}_j\right|^2, 
\quad \operatorname{Im} z_l>0</math>For <math>\beta = 1</math>, the <math>N \times N</math> matrix has <math>N</math> complex eigenvalues, and each eigenvalue has a conjugate that is also an eigenvalue. However, they may no longer come in conjugate ''pairs'', since some eigenvalues may be purely real. It is not even absolutely continuous, thus does not have a probability density function, but decomposes into sectors depending on the number of real eigenvalues.<ref name=":1" /> However, at the <math>N \to \infty</math> limit, the circular law is recovered, since there are only <math>O(\sqrt N)</math>  eigenvalues exactly on the real line.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Edelman |first1=Alan |chapter=Random Matrix Theory and Its Innovative Applications |date=2013 |title=Advances in Applied Mathematics, Modeling, and Computational Science |pages=91–116 |editor-last=Melnik |editor-first=Roderick |place=Boston, MA |publisher=Springer US |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-5389-5_5 |isbn=978-1-4614-5389-5 |last2=Wang |first2=Yuyang |editor2-last=Kotsireas |editor2-first=Ilias S.|hdl=1721.1/115827 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Determinantal point process ===
For <math>\beta = 2</math>, the eigenvalues make up a [[determinantal point process]]<math display="block">\rho_{(k), N}\left(z_1, \ldots, z_k\right)=\det\left[K_N\left(z_j, z_l\right)\right]_{j, l=1}^k</math>with correlation kernel<math display="block">K_N(w, z)=\frac{1}{\pi} e^{-\left(|w|^2+|z|^2\right) / 2} \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{(w \bar{z})^{j-1}}{(j-1)!}=\frac{1}{\pi} e^{-\left(|w|^2+|z|^2\right) / 2} e^{w \bar{z}} \frac{\Gamma(N ; w \bar{z})}{\Gamma(N)}</math>where <math>\Gamma(j ; x)=\int_x^{\infty} t^{j-1} e^{-t} d t</math> denotes the [[Incomplete gamma function|upper incomplete gamma function]]. It has the following asymptotics<math display="block">K_{\infty}^{\mathrm{b}}(w, z):=\lim _{N \rightarrow \infty} K_N(w, z)=\frac{1}{\pi} e^{-\left(|w|^2+|z|^2\right) / 2} e^{w \bar{z}},</math><math display="block">K_{\infty}^{\mathrm{e}}\left(z_1, z_2\right):=\lim _{N \rightarrow \infty} K_N\left(-i \sqrt{N}+z_1,-i \sqrt{N}+z_2\right)=e^{-\left(\left|z_1\right|^2+\left|z_2\right|^2\right) / 2} e^{z_1 \bar{z}_2} h\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(-i z_1+i \bar{z}_2\right)\right)</math>where <math>h(z)=\frac{1}{2 \pi}(1+\operatorname{erf}(\sqrt{2} z))</math>.

=== Global law ===
[[File:Eigenvalue density of Ginibre.svg|thumb|Plot of <math display="inline">\pi\rho(z)</math> for varying values of <math>N</math>. It rapidly converges to the uniform distribution.]]
Plugging in the correlation kernel, the average distribution of all eigenvalues is<math display="block">\frac 1N K_N(z, z) = \frac{\Gamma(N; |z|^2)}{\pi N!} = \frac{\int_{|z|^2}^\infty t^{N-1} e^{-t}dt}{\pi N!}</math>Scaling down by <math>\sqrt N</math>, we find that the average distribution of the eigenvalues of <math display="inline">\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} G_N</math> to have probability density function <math display="block">\rho(z) = \frac{N^N}{\pi (N-1)!} \int_{|z|^2}^\infty t^{N-1} e^{-Nt} dt</math>which rapidly converges to <math>\begin{cases}\frac 1\pi & \text{if }|z| < 1 \\ 0 & \text{if }|z| > 1\end{cases}</math>.[[File:CircleLaw.png|thumb|Plot of the real and imaginary parts (scaled by sqrt(1000)) of the eigenvalues of a 1000x1000 matrix with independent, standard normal entries.]]More strongly, we have the strong global law. Let <math>(G_N)_{N=1}^\infty</math> be a sequence sampled from the complex Ginibre ensemble. Define <math>\displaystyle \mu_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} G_n}</math> to be the [[Empirical spectral measures|empirical spectral measure]] of <math display="inline">\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} G_N</math>. Then, [[almost surely]] (i.e. with probability one), the sequence of measures [[Convergence in distribution|converges in distribution]] to the uniform measure on the unit disk.

=== As a Coulomb gas ===
Recall the spectral distribution<math display="block">\rho_N\left(z_1, \ldots, z_N\right)=\frac{1}{Z} \exp \left(-\sum_{k=1}^N\left|z_k\right|^2\right) \prod_{1 \leq j<k \leq N}\left|z_j-z_k\right|^2</math>It can be interpreted as the [[Boltzmann distribution]] for a [[Coulomb gas]], or more specifically a two-dimensional one-component plasma (OCP), at [[Thermodynamic beta|inverse temperature]] <math>\beta = 2</math>. Note that here <math>\beta </math> is used to mean something different, and may take any value within <math>(0, \infty)</math>.

The gas contains <math>N</math> identical particles, all placed within the plane <math>\mathbb C</math>, with total energy<math display="block">E = \frac 12 \sum_{k=1}^N |z_k|^2 - \sum_{1 \leq j < k \leq N} \ln |z_j - z_k|</math>The first term indicates that every particle is attracted to the origin by a force of magnitude <math>F_k = |z_k|</math>. The second term indicates that every particle pair is repelling each other by a force of magnitude <math>F_{jk} = \frac{1}{|z_j - z_k|} </math>.

For general inverse temperature <math>\beta</math>, the OCP has partition function <math>Z_{N}^{\text{OCP}}(\beta) = \int_{\mathbb C^N} e^{-\beta E} d^Nz </math>, and [[Helmholtz free energy|free energy]] <math>-\beta^{-1} \ln Z_{\beta, N}^{\text{OCP}} </math>. However, it is theoretically more natural to consider the normalized partition function <math display="block">Z_N^{D_R, \mathrm{OCP}}(\beta)=\frac{1}{N!} A_{N, \beta} Z_N^{\mathrm{OCP}}(\beta), \quad A_{N, \beta}=e^{-\beta N^2\left(\frac{1}{4} \log N-\frac{3}{8}\right)} </math>where the <math>N! </math> part accounts for the fact that the particles are indistinguishable from each other, and <math>A_{N,\beta} </math> removes the [[self-energy]] of the average plasma, that is, the self-energy of a disk of radius <math>R = \sqrt N </math> and charge density <math>\frac{1}{\pi} </math>. Thus, <math>Z_N^{D_R, \mathrm{OCP}}(\beta) </math> is the partition function of a "charge neutral" OCP.<ref name=":1" />

The log-partition function satisfies<math display="block">-\ln Z_N^{D_R, \mathrm{OCP}}(\beta)\Big|_{\beta=2}=N \beta f(\beta)\Big|_{\beta=2}+\frac{1}{12} \ln N-\zeta^{\prime}(-1)-\frac{1}{720 N^2}+O\left(\frac{1}{N^4}\right)</math>where <math>\beta f(\beta)\Big|_{\beta=2}=\frac{1}{2} \log \left(\frac{1}{2 \pi^3}\right)</math> is the average free energy per particle at the <math>N \to \infty</math> limit. It is conjectured that for general <math>\beta</math>,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Can |first1=T. |last2=Forrester |first2=P. J. |last3=Téllez |first3=G. |last4=Wiegmann |first4=P. |date=March 2015 |title=Exact and Asymptotic Features of the Edge Density Profile for the One Component Plasma in Two Dimensions |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10955-014-1152-2 |journal=Journal of Statistical Physics |language=en |volume=158 |issue=5 |pages=1147–1180 |doi=10.1007/s10955-014-1152-2 |arxiv=1310.3130 |bibcode=2015JSP...158.1147C |issn=0022-4715}}</ref><math display="block">-\ln Z_N^{D_R, \mathrm{OCP}}(\beta)=N \beta f(\beta)\Big|_{\beta=2} + \frac{4 \log (\beta / 2)}{3 \pi^{1 / 2}} \sqrt N + \frac{1}{12} \ln N + O(1)</math>

=== Microscopic law ===

== Large deviation theory ==
Let <math>G_n</math> be sampled from the real or complex ensemble, and let <math>\rho(G_n)</math> be the absolute value of its maximal eigenvalue:<math display="block">\rho(G_n) := \max_j |\lambda_j|</math>We have the following theorem for the edge statistics:<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Rider |first=B |date=2003-03-28 |title=A limit theorem at the edge of a non-Hermitian random matrix ensemble |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0305-4470/36/12/331 |journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General |volume=36 |issue=12 |pages=3401–3409 |doi=10.1088/0305-4470/36/12/331 |bibcode=2003JPhA...36.3401R |issn=0305-4470|url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{Math theorem
| math_statement = For <math>G_n</math> and <math>\rho\left(G_n\right)</math> as above, with probability one,
<math display=block>\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \rho\left(G_n\right)=1</math>

Moreover, let <math>\gamma_n=\log \left(\frac{n}{2 \pi}\right)-2 \log (\log (n))</math>, then <math>\sqrt{4 n \gamma_n}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \rho\left(G_n\right)-1-\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_n}{4 n}}\right),</math> converges in distribution to the [[Gumbel law]], i.e., the probability measure on <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with cumulative distribution function <math>F_{\mathrm{Gum}}(x)=e^{-e^{-x}}</math>.

Furthermore, for any <math>M, \delta > 0</math>, almost surely <math>\frac{1}{\sqrt n} \rho(G_n) \in 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt n} [M, (2 + \delta) \sqrt{\ln n}]</math> for all large <math>n</math>.

The theorem still holds for quaternionic non-Hermitian matrix ensembles, with <math>e^{-e^{-x}}</math> replaced by <math>e^{-\sqrt 2 e^{-x}}</math>.
| name = Edge statistics of the Ginibre ensemble
| note = 
}}

This theorem refines the circular law of the Ginibre ensemble. In words, the circular law says that the spectrum of <math>\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} G_n</math> almost surely falls uniformly on the unit disc.  and the edge statistics theorem states that the radius of the almost-unit-disk is about <math>1 + \sqrt{\frac{\gamma_n}{4 n}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{4 n \gamma_n}} z </math>, where <math>z </math> is a random variable sampled from the standard Gumbel distribution.

==History==

For random matrices with Gaussian distribution of entries (the ''Ginibre ensembles''), the circular law was established in the 1960s by [[Jean Ginibre]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ginibre|first=Jean|title=Statistical ensembles of complex, quaternion, and real matrices|journal=J. Math. Phys.|year=1965|volume=6|issue=3 |pages=440–449|doi=10.1063/1.1704292|mr=0173726|bibcode=1965JMP.....6..440G}}</ref> In the 1980s, Vyacheslav Girko introduced<ref>{{cite journal|last=Girko|first=V.L.|title=The circular law|journal=Teoriya Veroyatnostei i ee Primeneniya|year=1984|volume=29|issue=4|pages=669–679}}</ref>  an approach which allowed to establish the circular law for more general distributions. Further progress was made<ref>{{cite journal|last=Bai|first=Z.D.|title=Circular law|journal=Annals of Probability|year=1997|volume=25|issue=1|pages=494–529|doi=10.1214/aop/1024404298|mr=1428519|doi-access=}}</ref>  by Zhidong Bai, who established the circular law under certain smoothness assumptions on the distribution.

The assumptions were further relaxed in the works of [[Terence Tao]] and [[Van H. Vu]],<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tao|first1=T.|last2=Vu|first2=V.H.|title=Random matrices: the circular law.|journal=Commun. Contemp. Math.|year=2008|volume=10|issue=2|pages=261–307|doi=10.1142/s0219199708002788|mr=2409368|arxiv=0708.2895|s2cid=15888373 }}</ref> Guangming Pan and Wang Zhou,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Pan|first1=G.|last2=Zhou|first2=W.|title=Circular law, extreme singular values and potential theory.|journal=J. Multivariate Anal.|year=2010|volume=101|issue=3|pages=645–656|doi=10.1016/j.jmva.2009.08.005|arxiv=0705.3773|s2cid=7475359 }}</ref> and Friedrich Götze and Alexander Tikhomirov.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Götze|first1=F.|last2=Tikhomirov|first2=A.|title=The circular law for random matrices|journal=Annals of Probability|year=2010|volume=38|issue=4|pages=1444–1491|doi=10.1214/09-aop522|mr=2663633|arxiv=0709.3995|s2cid=1290255 }}</ref> Finally, in 2010 Tao and Vu proved<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tao|first1=Terence|author1-link=Terence Tao|last2=Vu|first2=Van|author2-link=Van Vu|title=Random matrices: Universality of ESD and the Circular Law|others=appendix by Manjunath Krishnapur|journal=Annals of Probability|volume=38|issue=5|year=2010|pages=2023–2065|arxiv=0807.4898|doi=10.1214/10-AOP534|mr=2722794|s2cid=15769353 }}</ref> the circular law under the minimal assumptions stated above.

The circular law result was extended in 1985 by Girko<ref>{{cite journal|last=Girko|first=V.L.|title=The elliptic law|journal=Teoriya Veroyatnostei i ee Primeneniya|year=1985|volume=30|pages=640–651}}</ref> to an elliptical law for ensembles of matrices with a fixed amount of correlation between the entries above and below the diagonal. The elliptic and circular laws were further generalized by Aceituno, Rogers and Schomerus to the hypotrochoid law which includes higher order correlations.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Aceituno|first1=P.V.|last2=Rogers|first2=T.|last3=Schomerus|first3=H.|title=Universal hypotrochoidic law for random matrices with cyclic correlations.|journal=Physical Review E|year=2019|volume=100|issue=1|article-number=010302|doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.100.010302 |pmid=31499759 |arxiv=1812.07055 |bibcode=2019PhRvE.100a0302A |s2cid=119325369 }}</ref>
